question: Can you explain efficent finetuning with lora?

slides.title: The Frozen Linear Layer
slides.caption: y = Wx
slides.narration: Start with a simple layer. The input vector x passes through the original weight matrix W and produces y. In LoRA, this original matrix stays frozen.

slides.title: Full Fine-Tuning
slides.caption: W' = W + \Delta W
slides.narration: Ordinary fine-tuning learns a change called delta W. The new matrix is the old matrix W plus that full update, so the update has the same dimensions as W.

slides.title: A Smaller Update
slides.caption: W' = W + BA
slides.narration: LoRA replaces the large update with two smaller matrices. A compresses the input into only r directions, and B expands those directions back to the output space.

slides.title: How LoRA Computes
slides.caption: W'x = (W + BA)x = Wx + B(Ax)
slides.narration: The adapted layer has two contributions. The frozen path computes Wx. The adapter path first computes Ax, then B of Ax. Adding them gives exactly the adapted output.

slides.title: Counting the Full Matrix
slides.caption: N_W = d_{\mathrm{out}}d_{\mathrm{in}}
slides.narration: A matrix with d_out rows and d_in columns contains d_out times d_in entries. Full fine-tuning must learn an update with all of those entries.

slides.title: Counting the Adapter
slides.caption: N_{\mathrm{LoRA}} = rd_{\mathrm{in}} + d_{\mathrm{out}}r = r(d_{\mathrm{in}}+d_{\mathrm{out}})
slides.narration: A has r times d_in entries. B has d_out times r entries. Add those two small matrices, and the trainable LoRA count is r times the sum of the layer dimensions.

slides.title: A Concrete Example
slides.caption: N_W = 4\cdot 3 = 12, \qquad N_{\mathrm{LoRA}} = 1(3+4)=7
slides.narration: Take a four-by-three layer and rank one. The full matrix has twelve entries. A has three, B has four, so the adapter has seven trainable entries.

slides.title: The Parameter Fraction
slides.caption: \frac{N_{\mathrm{LoRA}}}{N_W} = \frac{r(d_{\mathrm{in}}+d_{\mathrm{out}})}{d_{\mathrm{out}}d_{\mathrm{in}}}
slides.narration: Seven out of twelve entries are trained in this small example, or about fifty-eight percent. Equivalently, the parameter count is reduced by about forty-two percent. Larger layers and smaller ranks make the advantage much bigger.

slides.title: Less Update Computation
slides.caption: C_{\mathrm{full}}=d_{\mathrm{out}}d_{\mathrm{in}}, \qquad C_{\mathrm{LoRA}}=r(d_{\mathrm{in}}+d_{\mathrm{out}})
slides.narration: A full update uses work proportional to d_out times d_in. LoRA uses two smaller products, with work proportional to r times d_in plus d_out times r. When r is small, the update is cheaper to apply.

slides.title: Memory and Storage Savings

rows: freeze W; train A and B
gradients only for A and B

slides.caption: W' = W + BA, \qquad \text{trainable parameters}=r(d_{\mathrm{in}}+d_{\mathrm{out}})
slides.narration: During training, gradients and optimizer states are needed for A and B, but not for the frozen W. The task-specific file is also much smaller: share the base model once, then attach a different small adapter for each task.

slides.title: FINAL ANSWER
slides.caption: \boxed{W' = W + BA,\qquad N_{\mathrm{trainable}} = r(d_{\mathrm{in}}+d_{\mathrm{out}}),\qquad \frac{N_{\mathrm{trainable}}}{N_{\mathrm{full}}}=\frac{r(d_{\mathrm{in}}+d_{\mathrm{out}})}{d_{\mathrm{out}}d_{\mathrm{in}}}}
slides.narration: LoRA keeps W frozen and trains only A and B. Their product BA is the learned low-rank update, so W'x equals Wx plus B(Ax). The adapter has r(d_in+d_out) trainable parameters instead of d_out d_in. When r is much smaller than both dimensions, this means less gradient and optimizer memory, cheaper update computation, and a much smaller task-specific adapter.
